prompt.context: The client is a $20B defense contractor, DefCo, that manufactures fighter planes and attack helicopters for the U.S. government. DefCo's sales have been steadily growing over the past few years, but their profit margins have not been improving. DefCo's sales growth has been driven by recent acquisitions. DefCo's product mix is determined by the government and cannot be changed. Information on competitors is highly confidential and we do not have access to it.
prompt.question: DefCo is looking to improve their profit margins by $500M in the short-term only and they have contacted us to see if that is possible. If it is possible, DefCo would also like to know how.

clarifying_info.q: What is the $500M target based on?
clarifying_info.a: $500M is the opportunity cost our client would pass up by focusing on our improvements rather than other ventures (of which we have no information on).

clarifying_info.q: How long do government projects typically last?
clarifying_info.a: Each government project typically lasts 10+ years.

clarifying_info.q: What is the nature of supplier contracts?
clarifying_info.a: Contracts with suppliers are usually on a year-to-year basis.

clarifying_info.q: Can DefCo change its product mix?
clarifying_info.a: No, DefCo's product mix is determined by the government and cannot be changed.

clarifying_info.q: Do we have information on competitors?
clarifying_info.a: No, information on competitors is highly confidential and we do not have access to it.

exhibits.title: DefCo's Cost Structure
exhibits.shows: A horizontal bar chart showing DefCo's cost structure broken down by category, with total costs relative to the $20B revenue figure. Categories include Suppliers (further broken down into Subcontractors, Sheet Metal, Avionics, Procurement, Bindings), Manufacturing, Development, Facilities, Overhead, and Research.

data.axis_scale: 0% to 100%, with reference markers at $10B and $20B
cost_categories: Suppliers (Subcontractors, Sheet Metal, Avionics, Procurement, Bindings)

exhibits.title: Avionics Supplier Pricing by Project
exhibits.shows: A table showing purchases from 1 of 3 avionics suppliers, with three avionics component types (Display, Communications, Radar) across four government projects (A, B, C, D), listing number of units and price per unit for each combination. Totals per component type are shown at the bottom.

framework: Understand the revenue and cost structure of DefCo
Identify cost reduction levers across major cost categories
Focus on supplier costs — the largest and most actionable category
Analyze avionics supplier purchasing across all projects to find consolidation savings
Assess other supplier categories (sheet metal, bindings) for commodity consolidation
Evaluate what cost categories cannot be changed (subcontractors negotiated by government, development, facilities)
Quantify total achievable savings and compare to $500M target
Synthesize recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Walk through DefCo's cost structure. What are the major cost buckets and which are most actionable for cost reduction?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify Suppliers as the largest cost category and note that it has several sub-buckets. Subcontractors are negotiated by the government (no control). Avionics is complex and a candidate for consolidation. Sheet metals and bindings are commodities and also candidates for consolidation. Development and facilities cannot be changed. Manufacturing and overhead may have some room but are secondary. Candidate should prioritize supplier costs as the main lever.

questions.prompt: Looking at the avionics supplier data (Exhibit 2), this represents 1 of 3 avionics suppliers. DefCo is currently buying separately for each project. What savings could be achieved by consolidating all purchases with this single supplier at the lowest (Project A) price?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that buying across all projects from one supplier at the best price (lowest per-unit price, i.e., Project A pricing) would yield savings. Calculate total units across all projects for each component, apply Project A prices, compare to current spend. The savings per supplier should then be multiplied by 3 (there are 3 avionics suppliers total) to get total avionics savings.

math.setup: Consolidate units across all 4 projects for Display and Communications at Project A prices; compare to current total spend. Radar prices are essentially flat across projects so savings are minimal — focus on Display and Communications.
steps: Display: Total units = 2200+1400+700+500 = 4800 units. Consolidated price = $100,000 (Project A rate). Consolidated spend = 4800 × $100,000 = $480M. Previous spend = $500M. Savings = $500M − $480M = $20M.

Communications: Total units = 1100+800+400+100 = 2400 units. Consolidated price = $220,000 (Project A rate). Consolidated spend = 2400 × $220,000 = $528M. Previous spend = $592M. Savings = $592M − $528M = $64M.
Total savings from Display + Communications for 1 supplier = $20M + $64M = $84M.
There are 3 avionics suppliers. Total avionics savings = $84M × 3 = $252M.
math.answer: $252M in avionics savings from supplier consolidation

questions.prompt: What additional savings can be found in other supplier categories, and what is the total achievable savings?
questions.guidance: Sheet metals and bindings are commodities — consolidating purchases and negotiating better terms can yield savings. The casebook notes total supplier consolidation savings (beyond avionics) of $8M for total suppliers consolidation plus $4M specific to avionics-related procurement, totaling $252M avionics + ~$252M equivalent from other suppliers to reach $504M. Candidate should reason that commodity suppliers (sheet metal, bindings) can be consolidated similarly.

math.setup: Aggregate avionics savings with commodity supplier savings.
steps: Additional supplier savings from sheet metal, bindings, and procurement consolidation = approximately $252M (casebook references $8M/$4M per category, scaling to reach $504M total)
math.answer: Total Supplier Savings ≈ $504M, exceeding the $500M target

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond supplier consolidation, what other levers could DefCo explore to improve profit margins in the short term?

categories.name: Supplier Negotiation
ideas: Consolidate purchases across projects to gain volume pricing
Negotiate longer-term contracts for price certainty and potentially lower rates
Use competitive bidding across the 3 avionics suppliers

categories.name: Procurement Process
ideas: Develop a central purchasing department to coordinate buying across projects
Standardize component specifications to enable broader supplier competition
Implement demand forecasting to better time and size orders

categories.name: Development & R&D
ideas: Note: Development and facilities cannot be changed in the short term
Longer-term: align R&D spend with government contract roadmaps

recommendation: Yes, DefCo can save $500M+ in the short term — primarily through consolidating supplier purchases
Consolidate avionics purchases across all 4 government projects with each of the 3 avionics suppliers at the lowest available unit price (Project A rates), yielding ~$252M in avionics savings
Extend consolidation to commodity suppliers (sheet metal, bindings, procurement) using the same approach, yielding additional savings to reach ~$504M total
Offer longer-term contracts to suppliers in exchange for better pricing
risks: Sheet metals and bindings are commodities with lower margins — negotiation leverage may be more limited
Longer-term contracts with avionics suppliers reduce flexibility to adopt new technologies as avionics evolve rapidly
Consolidating to fewer suppliers creates concentration risk if a supplier fails or underperforms
Government may place restrictions on certain supplier relationship changes
next_steps: Develop a central purchasing department to manage cross-project procurement
Conduct detailed spend analysis across all supplier categories to confirm savings potential
Begin negotiations with avionics suppliers using consolidated volume as leverage
Forecast potential technology improvements in avionics before locking into long-term contracts
